title: The birth of American jazz
subject: art
description: Born in New Orleans, jazz blended African rhythms, the blues, and European harmony, then invented swing, bebop, and modal jazz.

hero.hook: In one port city, America invented its own classical music: jazz.

blocks.text: Jazz was born in [[New Orleans]] toward the end of the 19th century. A Louisiana port and a crossroads of French, Spanish, African, and Caribbean life, the city was a laboratory of sound.

Born out of the violence of slavery and segregation, this music became “America's classical music.” In a single century it shaped rock, funk, and hip-hop. To understand jazz is to understand a freedom invented under constraint.

At the end of the 19th century, New Orleans mixed Creoles of color, descendants of enslaved Africans, and European immigrants. European opera met Caribbean rhythms. At [[Congo Square]], the one place in North America where Black people could gather on Sundays, African drums and polyrhythms survived.

blocks.caption: Congo Square: African rhythmic memory at the heart of Louisiana

blocks.text: **Brass bands** carried the parades and the funerals: a slow march to the cemetery, an explosion of joy on the way back. That swing between mourning and celebration is the emotional soul of early jazz.
The pioneer **Buddy Bolden**, a barber by trade, was never recorded. His legend rests on the people who heard his cornet from the other side of the Mississippi.

sections.title: Blue notes, improvisation, and Jim Crow

blocks.text: Jazz took its [[blue notes]] from the blues, bent notes that create an expressive tension. From gospel and work songs it took call and response. All of it sat on top of the European harmony of the brass bands.

The real break was [[Improvisation in jazz]]: the score stopped being a law and became a grid. The musician composes in real time. In the America of [[Jim Crow laws]], that freedom was political too, a way of asserting who you are when the system wants to erase you.
In 1917, the first jazz record was cut by white musicians, the Original Dixieland Jass Band. The labels did not yet dare to bet on the Black inventors of the music.

sections.title: Armstrong, swing, bebop, Kind of Blue

blocks.text: With the [[Great Migration]] toward Chicago and New York, jazz left the South. **Louis Armstrong** put the virtuoso soloist at the center. In Harlem, during the [[Harlem Renaissance]], jazz was celebrated as Black modernity. In the 1930s, the [[swing]] of **Duke Ellington** got America dancing.

blocks.caption: Louis Armstrong: the soloist becomes the heart of jazz

blocks.text: After 1945, **Charlie Parker** invented [[bebop]]: fast tempos, complex harmonies, music made for listening. In **1959**, **Miles Davis** released *Kind of Blue*, where [[modal jazz]] slows the chord changes to explore a single color. It is still the best-selling jazz record in the world.

blocks.caption: Kind of Blue (1959): modal jazz, calm and revolutionary

blocks.text: The New York club Birdland took its name from Parker's nickname, “Bird.” Parker himself was thrown out of it one night after an argument.

In the 1960s, [[free jazz]] broke the frames, tied to the fight for civil rights. Then [[jazz fusion]] crossed the music with electric rock and funk. Swing, that elastic pulse, still runs through rock and hip-hop. Taught in conservatories today, jazz remains a language of the moment: every concert is unique.
